section.title: The Lamb and the Harvest of the Earth
section.sectionRationale: Chapter 14 directly answers chapter 13. Where the beast marked and coerced worship from those who dwell on the earth, the Lamb stands with 144,000 marked with His own name and His Father's; where the beast demanded false worship through deceptive signs, three flying angels proclaim the true, eternal gospel, announce Babylon's fall, and warn of the wrath awaiting the beast's worshipers; and the chapter closes with two harvest scenes, grain gathered and grapes trodden, that resolve the whole conflict into ingathering and judgment.
section.thesis: Against the beast's mark and forced worship, the Lamb keeps His own people, marked with His name and His Father's; three angels proclaim the eternal gospel, Babylon's fall, and the certainty of wrath for the beast's worshipers; and the chapter ends with the earth's two harvests, grain for the redeemed and grapes for the wicked, trodden in the great winepress of God's wrath.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the Lamb and the 144,000 on Mount Zion; the three angels proclaiming the gospel, Babylon's fall, and the warning of wrath; the beatitude on those who die in the Lord; the harvest of grain; and the harvest of grapes trodden in the winepress of wrath.

units.label: The Lamb and the 144,000 on Zion
units.note: the redeemed, marked with the Lamb's name

verses.text: Then I looked and saw the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with Him 144,000 who had His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads.
And I heard a sound from heaven like the roar of many waters and the loud rumbling of thunder. And the sound I heard was like harpists strumming their harps.
And they sang a new song before the throne and before the four living creatures and the elders. And no one could learn the song except the 144,000 who had been redeemed from the earth.

These are the ones who have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins. They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as {{aparche|firstfruits}} to God and to the Lamb.
And no lie was found in their mouths; they are blameless.

units.label: Three angels: gospel, Babylon's fall, and the warning of wrath
units.note: a last call before the harvest

verses.text: Then I saw another angel flying overhead, with the eternal {{euangelion|gospel}} to proclaim to those who dwell on the earth, to every nation and tribe and tongue and people.
And he said in a loud voice, “Fear God and give Him glory, because the hour of His judgment has come. Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters.”
Then a second angel followed, saying, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, who has made all the nations drink the wine of the {{thymos|passion}} of her immorality.”
And a third angel followed them, calling out in a loud voice, “If anyone worships the beast and its image, and receives its mark on his forehead or on his hand,
he too will drink the wine of God's anger, poured undiluted into the cup of His {{orge|wrath}}. And he will be tormented in fire and sulfur in the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb.
And the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever. Day and night there is no rest for those who worship the beast and its image, or for anyone who receives the mark of its name.”
Here is a call for the perseverance of the saints who keep the commandments of God and the faith of Jesus.

units.label: Blessed are the dead in the Lord

verses.text: And I heard a voice from heaven telling me to write, “Blessed are the dead, those who die in the Lord from this moment on.” “Yes,” says the Spirit, “they will rest from their labors, for their deeds will follow them.”

units.label: The harvest of grain
units.note: the Son of Man swings the sickle

verses.text: And I looked and saw a white cloud, and seated on the cloud was One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown on His head and a sharp sickle in His hand.

Then another angel came out of the temple, crying out in a loud voice to the One seated on the cloud, “Swing Your sickle and {{therizo|reap}}, because the time has come to harvest; for the crop of the earth is ripe.”
So the One seated on the cloud swung His sickle over the earth, and the earth was harvested.

units.label: The harvest of grapes and the winepress of wrath

verses.text: Then another angel came out of the temple in heaven, and he too had a sharp sickle.

Still another angel, with authority over the fire, came from the altar and called out in a loud voice to the angel with the sharp sickle, “Swing your sharp sickle and gather the clusters of grapes from the vine of the earth, because its grapes are ripe.”
So the angel swung his sickle over the earth and gathered the grapes of the earth, and he threw them into the great winepress of God's wrath.
And the winepress was trodden outside the city, and the blood that flowed from it rose as high as the bridles of the horses for a distance of 1,600 stadia.

aparche.gloss: Firstfruits, the first and consecrated portion of a larger harvest, offered to God under the law before the rest of the crop was used, Leviticus 23:10. The 144,000 are called firstfruits, a first, representative portion of a much larger redeemed harvest still to be gathered, belonging to God and to the Lamb.

euangelion.gloss: Good news, gospel. Here it is called the eternal gospel, proclaimed by an angel to every nation, tribe, tongue, and people, the same good news of God's saving purpose in Christ that stands unchanged from before the foundation of the world into the hour of final judgment.

thymos.gloss: Passion, fury, intense anger poured out. It describes both Babylon's intoxicating wine of immoral passion, which she forces the nations to drink, and God's own wine of anger, poured back on those who drink hers, a deliberate reversal in which the earth's seducer is answered in kind.

orge.gloss: Settled, righteous wrath, as distinct from a sudden outburst. It names the contents of the cup poured undiluted for those who worship the beast, God's just and unmixed judgment against persistent, willful sin, held in reserve until this hour.

therizo.gloss: To reap or harvest. The One like the Son of Man is told to swing His sickle and reap because the crop of the earth is ripe, the same verb used of gathering a field of grain, here applied to the final ingathering at the close of the age.

basic.context: This chapter directly answers chapter 13. Instead of the beast's mark, the Lamb's own people stand with Him on Mount Zion, marked with His name and His Father's. Three angels fly overhead proclaiming the eternal gospel to every nation, announcing the fall of Babylon, and warning that anyone who worships the beast will drink God's undiluted wrath. The chapter ends with two harvest scenes: grain gathered by the Son of Man, and grapes gathered and trodden in the great winepress of God's wrath.
basic.hermeneutics: Interpreters debate whether the 144,000 and their description as virgins should be read literally, as a specific, defined company, or symbolically, as a picture of the whole faithful church kept pure from spiritual adultery with Babylon. They likewise debate whether the grain harvest and grape harvest are two different outcomes, ingathering versus judgment, or one judgment scene told twice. Either way, the chapter's message is plain: the age will end in a definite, complete harvest, and no one is left ungathered.
basic.originalLanguages: The redeemed are called aparche, firstfruits, a first portion promising a larger harvest to come. An angel proclaims the euangelion, the eternal gospel, to every nation before judgment falls. Babylon's wine is called thymos, passion, and God answers it with His own thymos and orge, His settled, undiluted wrath. And the final ingathering is pictured with therizo, to reap, the ordinary word for harvesting a ripe field.
basic.typology: The firstfruits offering of the law, the first portion consecrated to God before the rest of the harvest, becomes a picture of the redeemed as the first installment of a far larger harvest still to come. The grain harvest, carried out by One like the Son of Man, echoes Jesus' own parables of a harvest at the end of the age, while the grape harvest fulfills Isaiah's picture of God alone treading the winepress of judgment.
basic.christ: The Lamb stands victorious with His marked people on Zion, and it is One like the Son of Man, Christ Himself, who is pictured swinging the sickle to gather the grain harvest, the ingathering of the redeemed. The eternal gospel proclaimed to every nation is fundamentally about Him, and even the wrath poured out is described as happening in the presence of the Lamb, showing that final judgment, no less than final salvation, belongs to Him.
basic.god: God's patience and God's justice appear together here. He sends His eternal gospel to every nation before judgment falls, giving fair warning through three angels, yet His wrath, once poured, is undiluted and complete, a cup of settled justice against a world that has traded worship of the Creator for worship of the beast and its image.
basic.crossReferences: Revelation 7:2-4 introduces the sealing of the 144,000 that this chapter assumes. Joel 3:13 supplies the picture of a ripe harvest and a full winepress. Matthew 13:24-30 and 36-43 tell of wheat and weeds gathered at the end of the age. And Isaiah 63:1-6 pictures the Lord alone treading the winepress of the nations in judgment.
basic.oneStory: Where the beast forced counterfeit worship and marked its followers for judgment, the Lamb keeps His own, marked with His true name, and sends His eternal gospel to every nation while there is still time to respond. The whole Bible moves toward this same twin ending, a harvest of ingathering for those who belong to Christ and a harvest of judgment for those who do not, both accomplished by the same Son of Man who once bore that judgment Himself.

context.literary:
Revelation 14 is a fourfold movement held together by a single question: who owns the earth? Verses 1 to 5 answer with a scene of possession, the Lamb on the mountain and a company who carry His name. Verses 6 to 13 answer with three angelic voices, each speaking in a loud voice, and then a short call to endurance and a beatitude that John is told to write down. Verses 14 to 20 answer with two reapings, the first by One like the Son of Man holding a sickle, the second by an angel who takes the clusters of the vine of the earth to the winepress. Notice how the chapter is built on interruption. Chapter 13 ended with a number and a call for wisdom, and chapter 14 breaks in with another number, 144,000, and another place, Zion, so that the reader is made to compare two sealed peoples side by side.

The three flying angels move from good news to news of ruin in a descending rhythm: worship the Creator, Babylon has fallen, the beast's worshipers will drink. Verse 12 is the hinge. It turns from what the angels say to what the saints must do, and verse 13 answers their endurance with a promise. The chapter also sets up a pointed symmetry, since the redeemed sing before the throne and have no lie in their mouths, while the beast's followers have the mark on forehead or hand. Finally, the harvest scenes are paired by a pattern John uses elsewhere, one scene for the people of God, one for their enemies, and the second reaping is the longer and the more terrible, flowing into the bowls of chapters 15 and 16.
context.historical:
John writes from Patmos to churches in Roman Asia where the pressure to join in emperor worship and civic cult was real, and where economic life ran through guilds whose feasts involved idols. Chapter 13 had described that pressure as a beast with a mark; chapter 14 is written to people tempted to think that refusal means losing everything. The first readers knew Mount Zion as the hill of Jerusalem where David's city stood and where the Lord had said He would set His king, Psalm 2:6. By the first century Zion had also become a way of speaking about God's final dwelling with His people, which is why Hebrews 12:22 can say believers have already come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God.

The harvest and the winepress belonged to everyday agricultural life, and the first hearers would have pictured both at once: the barley and wheat cut with a sickle in the spring and early summer, and the grape harvest at summer's end, when clusters were piled into a rock cut press and trodden by foot. These were the images the prophets already used for the nations. The place of treading, 'outside the city,' reminds Jewish readers of the place of judgment and of impurity, and Christians of the place where Jesus Himself was put to death, Hebrews 13:12. Babylon is named here, in the second angel's cry, without explanation, as though the churches would at once recognise the name for the power that sat over their world. The details are drawn from Isaiah's own Babylon oracle, which had been read in synagogues for centuries.
context.canonical:
The chapter is dense with the Old Testament. The cry 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon' repeats Isaiah 21:9 almost word for word, and the loud call to 'Fear God and give Him glory' recalls the Psalms' summons to the nations. The harvest and the winepress come from Joel 3:13 and Isaiah 63:2 to 3, where the Lord treads the winepress and His garments are stained. The vision of One like the Son of Man on a cloud is Daniel 7:13 reused, now with a golden crown and a sickle, so that the figure of Daniel's vindication becomes also the figure of the harvest.

Within Revelation, the chapter looks back to the sealing in 7:3 and 7:4, to the name on the forehead promised in 3:12, and to the beast's counter-mark in 13:16 and 13:17. It looks forward to 19:15, where the same Rider 'treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty,' to the fall of Babylon in chapter 18, and to 22:4, where the name is on the foreheads of those who see His face. The New Testament parallels are plentiful: the parables of the wheat and the weeds, and of the great harvest at the age's end in Matthew 13, and Jesus' own saying that the harvest is plentiful in Matthew 9:37. Paul calls the Spirit the firstfruits in Romans 8:23, and James calls believers a kind of firstfruits of His creatures in James 1:18, which shows that Revelation 14:4 is not an odd image but part of a larger apostolic vocabulary.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
John did not write chapter 14 to satisfy curiosity about the exact size of an army or the length of a battlefield. He wrote it so that believers under pressure could look from the beast's mark to the Lamb's name and decide which one they belonged to. The first hearers needed three things. They needed to be told who they were, a company who follow the Lamb wherever He goes and whose mouths are honest. They needed to be told that the world's story has an end, and that both the persecutors and the persecuted are inside it. And they needed a way to endure, which is why verse 12 speaks of perseverance and verse 13 pronounces a blessing on those who die in the Lord.

The three angels are an act of mercy as much as of warning. The gospel goes out before the judgment, to every nation and tribe and tongue and people, so that no one will be able to say the hour came without notice. John expects hearers to respond in worship and faithfulness: fear God, give Him glory, keep the commandments, hold to the faith of Jesus. The harvest scenes are meant to settle, in advance, the fear that evil has the last word.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Much of the chapter describes a heavenly scene, a number, a winepress and a river of blood, none of which is a command. What is prescribed is brief and clear: verse 7 gives the imperatives of the angel, fear God, give Him glory, worship the One who made the heavens and the earth, and verse 12 names the call for perseverance. The vision also carries a beatitude, verse 13, that is more promise than instruction. Care is needed with the description of the 144,000 as 'virgins' who 'have not been defiled with women.' It is not a rule for how every believer must live, since the New Testament elsewhere honours marriage, 1 Timothy 4:3 and Hebrews 13:4. The picture is of a company kept faithful, and the Old Testament habit of treating idolatry as adultery makes faithfulness the primary meaning.

In the same way, the description of torment in fire and sulfur is something John sees and reports, not an invitation to hatred. The churches are told to endure and to witness, not to take vengeance. Today the passage shapes how Christians hold hope and warning together: they proclaim the gospel to everyone, they refuse the world's counterfeit worship, and they leave judgment in the hands of the Son of Man.

debates.question: Who are the 144,000, and what does 'virgins' mean?

views.label: The whole redeemed church, described symbolically
views.case: The number is built from twelve times twelve times a thousand, and chapter 7 lists tribes in an unusual order, which suggests a figure for the complete people of God. John hears the number in 7:4 but sees 'a great multitude that no one could count' in 7:9, as if one company were being described in two ways. Their purity 'from women' then matches the Old Testament's picture of idolatry as adultery, and the 'name on their foreheads' is promised to every overcomer in 3:12 and 22:4. The word 'firstfruits' in verse 4 fits believers generally, as in James 1:18.

views.label: A distinct group, literal in number and in celibacy
views.case: The text does call them 'redeemed from among men,' it gives a precise number, and 'not defiled with women' reads naturally as a statement about sexual conduct. Some take them as a special company of Jewish believers, or of those consecrated to Christ in a particular way, and point out that the number is stated twice, in 7:4 and 14:1, with no hint that it is merely figurative.

views.label: A literal number of ethnic Israel, kept through the tribulation
views.case: On this view, chapter 7 explicitly names the twelve tribes, and the sealing of a remnant of Israel is a separate event from the multitude of Gentiles. The 144,000 on Zion are those same sealed Jews, now seen again, and the sexual language marks them as undefiled by the beast's religion.

debates.bearing: All three views agree that the company carries the Lamb's name, follows Him, and is kept from the beast's counterfeit. The same chapter pictures a people, not a spectacle, and it sets before every reader the question of whose name is on them. Whichever view is taken, the text does not make celibacy a requirement for belonging to Christ.

debates.question: Are the two harvests one event or two?

views.label: Two outcomes: ingathering and judgment
views.case: The first harvest is done by One like the Son of Man, with a golden crown, and the verb is simply 'the earth was harvested.' The second is done by an angel and ends in a winepress of wrath and a flood of blood. The imagery of grain and grapes is different, the agents are different, and the second is expressly 'God's wrath.' Matthew 13:30 and 13:41 to 43 also separate gathering the wheat from burning the weeds.

views.label: One judgment seen twice
views.case: Others note that Joel 3:13 puts sickle and winepress in one verse for one event, and that in Revelation the Son of Man's sickle in 14:14 to 16 gives no hint of salvation, only of ripeness. The two scenes then reinforce each other, the first the sweep of the whole earth, the second the detail of the treading, and both are the same final judgment.

views.label: The first is the gathering of the church, the second the judgment of the wicked
views.case: Because the angel in 14:15 says the 'crop of the earth is ripe,' and because 14:4 has just named the redeemed as firstfruits, the grain harvest is read as the final gathering of believers, parallel to Matthew 24:31, with the grape harvest as the punishment that follows.

debates.bearing: The ambiguity should not hide the plain claim: the Son of Man reaps, and the winepress of God's wrath is real. Judgment is not hidden from view or left to chance, and the passage forbids any reading in which evil simply wears itself out.

study.originalLanguages:
Beyond the words the basic level names, several small choices in the Greek carry weight. The verb for 'follow' in verse 4 is akoloutheo, the word Jesus used when He first called disciples, 'Follow Me.' Here it is in the present tense, so that the company are those who keep on following the Lamb wherever He goes, an ongoing pattern rather than a single decision. John uses the same verb at the end of verse 13: the deeds of those who die in the Lord 'follow' them. The followers of the Lamb are followed by their own works, and what began as a path becomes a record.

The adjective in verse 5, 'blameless,' is amomos. It is the ordinary Greek word for an animal without defect, the kind required of an offering in the Old Testament, and in the New Testament it describes Christ as an unblemished lamb in 1 Peter 1:19 and the church presented to Him in Ephesians 5:27. A company with no lie in their mouths are offered to God as a sacrifice without blemish, which fits the word firstfruits that comes just before it.

The word translated 'perseverance' in verse 12 is hypomone, literally a remaining under. It names the posture of someone who bears a weight and does not step out from it, and John uses it in 1:9 of himself and in 13:10 of the saints. Verse 13 then uses the root of the verb anapauo, 'rest,' for the blessed dead, and in verse 11 the same noun, anapausis, is denied to the beast's worshipers, who have 'no rest' day or night. The same word marks the saints' relief and the wicked's lack of it, a quiet contrast that English does not show.

The second angel's 'Fallen, fallen' is epesen epesen, the aorist tense, which speaks of the event as already settled even though Babylon still stands. It is the 'prophetic past,' the way Isaiah spoke in Isaiah 21:9. And the opening command of verse 7, 'Fear God and give Him glory,' uses two aorist imperatives, urgent and decisive, matched by the reason given: the hour of His judgment, krisis, has come. The cry to 'give Him glory' returns in 16:9, where people refuse it. Even the verb for harvest differs from the verb for gathering grapes, a small sign that two distinct actions are being pictured.

typology.fulfillment: Zion in the Old Testament is the hill where the Lord installs His king, Psalm 2:6, and the place nations are told will become the centre of worship, Isaiah 2:2. In Revelation 14 the king is the Lamb, and He stands on Zion not as a besieged ruler but as one who has already overcome. Hebrews 12:22 says believers have already come to Mount Zion, so the vision shows the present reality of their standing as well as the future. The type falls short on its own, since earthly Zion fell to Babylon and later to Rome; the Zion of the Lamb cannot be taken, and its people stand there with Him.

Israel offered the first sheaf of the harvest to the Lord, Leviticus 23:10, before eating any of the rest, a sign that the whole harvest belonged to Him. The 144,000 are called firstfruits 'to God and to the Lamb,' which places them as the part that is offered with the promise of more. Paul applies the same idea to Christ's own resurrection, 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and to the Spirit, Romans 8:23. The correspondence escalates: the first sheaf was grain, the firstfruits here are people, and behind them is the risen Christ. The type falls short where the sheaf was waved and eaten, while these are kept and sealed.

Isaiah 63:2 to 3 pictures the Lord coming from Edom with garments stained from treading the winepress alone, and Joel 3:13 calls on the nations to be trampled because their wickedness is great. Revelation 14:19 and 19:15 take the picture up and place it in the hands of the Lamb's own Rider. The escalation is that the stain on the garment is now the blood of the nations in an overflowing stream, and the One who treads is the one who first bled outside the city, Hebrews 13:12. The old picture is reused but also overturned, since the treading takes place 'outside the city,' not in a conquered Edom.

typology.type: The Son of Man on the cloud
typology.fulfillment: Daniel 7:13 shows one like a son of man coming with the clouds to receive dominion. Jesus applied that title to Himself before the high priest, Matthew 26:64, and John saw it at His first vision, Revelation 1:7 and 1:13. In 14:14 the figure holds a golden crown and a sickle, so that rule and harvest are joined. The type is not left behind but fulfilled: what Daniel saw as a vindication is also the Lord's act of gathering. The only limit of the correspondence is that Daniel saw a throne room in heaven, while Revelation has the One on the cloud swinging His sickle over the earth.

study.christ:
The Lamb is the first figure in the chapter, and the picture is deliberate: the one who was slain is now standing. In chapter 5 He was the Lamb 'looking as if slain,' and here He is on Zion with His people. The pattern of the whole chapter is that Christ is the owner of everyone in it. The 144,000 are His by purchase, 'redeemed,' and by name, since they bear His name and His Father's. The word 'redeemed' in verses 3 and 4 uses the language of the marketplace, the price paid for a slave or a captive, which is what the cross accomplished, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19. The beast could only mark; the Lamb has bought.

He is also the pattern for the company's life. They 'follow the Lamb wherever He goes,' which, in the Gospels, is what discipleship means, and in Revelation means going where He went, to the cross and through it, 12:11. Their blamelessness is not self made. It is the likeness of One whom Peter calls a lamb without blemish or defect.

The chapter then shows Christ as judge. The One seated on the cloud, with a golden crown and a sickle, is the same Son of Man who spoke of sending angels to gather the elect in Matthew 24:30 to 31, and who said the Son of Man would be seen coming on the clouds before the high priest, Matthew 26:64. The one who stood trial is now seated, and what He does with the sickle is the harvest He promised. It would be a mistake, though, to force the second harvest onto a single named person. The text gives that sickle to an angel and the winepress to 'God's wrath,' while 19:15 says the Rider treads it. The New Testament keeps both: God judges through His Son, John 5:22, and the Son judges as God.

Finally, the chapter offers the Lamb as the gospel itself. The 'eternal gospel' of verse 6 is not a different message from the one the apostles preached; it is the news that God has acted in Christ. Torment in 'the presence of the holy angels and of the Lamb' in verse 10 means that the Lamb is neither absent nor indifferent in the judgment. He is the one before whom everything is finally open, and the one who also says, in verse 13 through the Spirit, that those who die in Him are blessed.
study.god:
The chapter shows God as Creator, Judge and Rewarder, and it holds these together without apology. The first angel's call, 'Worship the One who made the heavens and the earth and the sea and the springs of waters,' draws on the Creator's claim in Exodus 20:11 and the commandments' own language, and it sets God's right to worship against the beast's. Worship is owed to the Maker, not to power. The same God who made the springs of water is the One who will turn rivers to blood in 16:4, so that creation itself is shown to belong to Him and to answer to His verdict.

The scene of the three angels reveals patience before judgment. God sends the gospel first, to every nation, tribe, tongue and people, and only then pronounces the hour. There is also precision. The angel who is 'over the fire' acts from the altar, so judgment is bound to the prayers and sacrifices of the saints, 6:9 and 8:3 to 5, rather than being random. The cup is 'poured undiluted,' which Greek speakers would hear against the practice of mixing wine with water. Mercy, in the sense of mixing or delay, has run its course, and what remains is the full strength of settled justice.

God is also seen as the keeper of His people. The 144,000 stand on Zion while the beast still rages, which tells hearers that preservation does not mean exemption from suffering. The blessing of verse 13 is spoken by the Spirit, so that death, which looks like the beast's victory, becomes a rest. Their deeds 'follow them,' and God neither forgets work done in His name nor leaves it unrewarded, Hebrews 6:10.

The tension that Revelation never resolves in a cheap way is that God's wrath is real and God's love is real. The text refuses to weaken either. Worship, for the believer, means seeing both: fear in the sense of reverence before the One who judges, and gladness that He is also the One who redeems. The doctrine of God that emerges from chapter 14 is that He is holy enough to judge the world, and faithful enough to hold a people to Himself through the judgment.

crossReferences.note: The source of the second angel's cry. Isaiah heard 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon' about the empire that conquered Jerusalem, and its idols lie shattered on the ground. John gives the same words to an angel because the pattern repeats: whatever power sets itself up as the world's centre will be brought down.

The sickle and the winepress in one verse. The harvest is ripe, the winepress full, and the vats overflow because wickedness is great. Revelation 14:15 and 14:18 use the same ripeness language, so John is taking Joel's picture of the Lord's day and showing how it is carried out.

The Lord's garments are stained from treading the winepress alone. This is the root of the image in verse 19, and 19:15 returns to it. The point is that judgment belongs to God alone, and that the nations' blood is the evidence of a completed verdict.

One like a son of man comes with the clouds and is given dominion. Revelation 14:14 uses the same figure and the same cloud, but adds a crown and a sickle. Daniel's vision of rule becomes John's vision of rule that gathers.

The sealing of the servants of God on their foreheads. Chapter 14 assumes this event and shows the sealed company safe with the Lamb. The seal in 7:3 is exactly the protection against the beast's mark in 13:16 to 17.

The beast's mark on the right hand or the forehead, without which no one may buy or sell. Chapter 14 sets the Lamb's name against it, so that every reader sees two brandings and must say which is theirs.

The parable of the wheat and the weeds, where the harvest is left until the end so that the two can be separated. Jesus explains that the harvest is the end of the age and the reapers are angels, which helps readers see why Revelation pictures sickles and angels.

Jesus suffered outside the gate to sanctify the people by His own blood. Revelation 14:20 says the winepress was trodden outside the city. The place of the cross and the place of the judgment are named in the same way, which invites readers to see how the two are connected.

Christ has been raised, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep. The firstfruits image in Revelation 14:4 sits against that: a first portion given to God which guarantees the rest, with Christ Himself as the first and surest.

The Rider treads the winepress of the fury of the wrath of God the Almighty. This is the fulfilment of the harvest of chapter 14, and shows that the One on the cloud and the Rider on the white horse are the one Lord of lords and King of kings.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with a garden and a command, and with a choice between obeying God and trusting another voice. Everything after that is a story of two peoples, those marked by the Serpent's lie and those who know the voice of their Shepherd, and chapter 14 is where the two are set side by side on the screen of history for the last time. Eden's tree and Babel's tower, Pharaoh's armies and Nebuchadnezzar's statue, all come to rest in this picture of the beast's mark and the Lamb's name. The question put in Genesis 3, whom will you trust and whom will you worship, is answered here with a flock on a mountain and a field being reaped.

The chapter also gathers the biblical language of harvest. From the first sheaf offered in the law to Jesus' parables of the field, from Joel's valley of decision to Isaiah's lone treader of the winepress, the Scriptures have used grain and grapes to speak of what God will do at the end of the age. Revelation does not invent these pictures but completes them. The gospel goes out to every nation, as God promised Abraham that all peoples on earth would be blessed through his offspring, Genesis 12:3, and then the harvest comes.

What the chapter sets up is the bowls, Babylon's fall, and the return of the King. Chapters 15 and 16 will empty the cup that the third angel warned about, chapter 18 will show Babylon's end, and chapter 19 will see the Rider and the winepress. And the chapter prepares the end of the story in the new creation: the people with the Lamb's name on their foreheads in 22:4, no longer needing to be sealed against a beast because the beast is gone. The mourning and the labour that verse 13 speaks of are over, and the redeemed rest. Between Eden and the city lie harvest and judgment, and the whole Bible says that they are God's work from first to last, with the Lamb at the centre.

quiz.q: Who stands with the Lamb on Mount Zion?

options.text: The 144,000, who have His name and His Father's name written on their foreheads.
options.note: Revelation 14:1 states this directly.

options.text: An unnamed crowd bearing the mark of the beast.
options.note: This group is marked with the Lamb's and the Father's names, the opposite of the beast's mark.

options.text: Only the twelve apostles.
options.note: The number is 144,000, not twelve individuals.

options.text: No one; the Lamb stands alone.
options.note: The text explicitly says 144,000 stand with Him.

quiz.q: What does the first of the three angels proclaim?

options.text: The eternal gospel, calling every nation to fear God and worship the Creator.
options.note: Revelation 14:6-7 describes this proclamation.

options.text: The immediate destruction of the whole earth.
options.note: The message is a call to worship and fear God, not an announcement of destruction.

options.text: A message meant only for the church, not the nations.
options.note: The gospel is proclaimed to every nation, tribe, tongue, and people.

options.text: Nothing; the first angel is silent.
options.note: The first angel proclaims the eternal gospel in a loud voice.

quiz.q: What does the second angel announce?

options.text: That Babylon the great has fallen, having made the nations drink the wine of her immorality.
options.note: Revelation 14:8 gives this announcement.

options.text: That Babylon has repented and been restored.
options.note: The announcement is Babylon's fall, not her restoration.

options.text: That the beast has repented of its blasphemy.
options.note: The announcement concerns Babylon's fall, not the beast's repentance.

options.text: Nothing about Babylon at all.
options.note: Babylon's fall is precisely what the second angel proclaims.

quiz.q: What does the beatitude in verse 13 promise to those who die in the Lord?

options.text: They are blessed, will rest from their labors, and their deeds will follow them.
options.note: Revelation 14:13 states this directly.

options.text: They will be forgotten along with their labors.
options.note: The opposite is promised; their deeds follow them and they rest.

options.text: They must continue laboring in the afterlife.
options.note: They are promised rest from their labors, not continued toil.

options.text: Nothing is said about those who die in the Lord.
options.note: The verse is a specific beatitude concerning exactly this group.

quiz.q: What do the two harvest scenes at the end of the chapter depict together?

options.text: A grain harvest and a grape harvest, widely read as the gathering of the redeemed and judgment on the wicked.
options.note: Revelation 14:14-20 presents both scenes, commonly read this way.

options.text: Two identical celebrations with no connection to judgment.
options.note: The grape harvest explicitly ends in the winepress of God's wrath.

options.text: A harvest that includes only angels, with no human significance.
options.note: Both harvests concern 'the earth' and its people, not angels alone.

options.text: Nothing; the chapter ends without any harvest imagery.
options.note: The final section is built entirely around two harvest scenes.

questions: The 144,000 are called firstfruits, a first portion promising a larger harvest to come. How does knowing you are part of something bigger than yourself shape how you live for Christ today?
An angel proclaims the eternal gospel to every nation before judgment falls. Who in your life still needs to hear that same good news from you while there is time?
Verse 13 promises rest and remembrance to those who die in the Lord. How does that promise change the way you think about weariness, labor, or even your own mortality?
Babylon offered an intoxicating counterfeit of satisfaction that God's wrath finally answers. What counterfeit comforts are you tempted to drink from instead of trusting God?
The chapter ends with a certain, complete harvest, no one is left ungathered. How does the certainty of that final harvest affect the urgency and hope with which you live this week?

translationNotes.note: Firstfruits, aparche, recalls the Israelite law of consecrating the first portion of a harvest to God, Leviticus 23:10; it pictures the 144,000 as a consecrated portion of a larger harvest still to come, not the entirety of the redeemed.

Babylon the great is named here for the first time in Revelation and is developed fully in chapters 17 and 18; the wine of the passion of her immorality pictures the intoxicating, seductive nature of the world system's idolatry.

'Poured undiluted' reflects that ancient wine was normally mixed with water; describing God's wrath as undiluted pictures judgment at full strength, unmixed with any admixture of mercy for the unrepentant.

1,600 stadia is roughly 184 miles or about 296 kilometers. Some read this as a literal distance connected to the length of the land, while others read 1,600 symbolically, as 40 multiplied by 40, a number associated elsewhere with testing and judgment.
